newsitem.title: USA: Clinton says he unaware of questionable donations.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says he unaware of questionable donations.

text.p: President Clinton said Tuesday he supported his legal defence fund's return of $640,000 in questionable contributions, in the latest embarrassing fundraising problem to trouble the White House.

Clinton, who was already under fire for Democratic Party fundraising tactics during the 1996 election cycle, said he was unaware that an old Arkansas acquaintance had been raising most of the sum in question until it came in.
"I supported the decision, I was aware of the decision to return the money," Clinton told reporters during a picture session with visiting Irish Prime Minister John Bruton.

The White House acknowledged that the acquaintance, Charles Yan Lin Trie, a naturalised American from Taiwan and Little Rock restauranteur who has known Clinton for 20 years, was at a White House Christmas party Friday and had a private conversation with Clinton.

Spokesman Mike McCurry went to great lengths during a long, testy briefing on the issue not to denounce Trie. He said the only motive he could ascribe to Trie was that he wanted to help an old friend in distress.

"It appears that an old friend of the president tried to lend some assistance to a president and a first lady who have a great deal of legal debt accumulated. That's the fact. The appearance is someone else's judgment to make," he said.

The legal fund's executive director, Michael Cardozo, announced Monday that about $640,000 in contributions had been returned or rejected after private investigators could not verify the sources of the funds.
Trie had given Cardozo two envelopes containing some $460,000 in questionable contributions last March 21.

The envelopes contained some checks and money orders written out in the same handwriting, even though they were supposed to have come from different people. Under rules set up by the trust fund, all donors must be U.S. citizens, must be clearly identified and cannot give more than $1,000 a year.
Cardozo said some of the donations also appeared to be linked to a Buddhist religious organisation known as Ching Hai, based in Taiwan.

"In all these fundraising endeavours the rules should be that all the checks should be checked to ensure that not only the fact but any, even, appearance of impropriety should be removed," Clinton said.
"And Mr. Cardozo was interested in the appearance of that and so was I and that's why the decision was made," he said.

He said his re-election campaign and defence fund had avoided any appearance of impropriety while noting the Democratic Party had acknowledged mistakes. "I think it was handled appropriately," he said of the defence fund.
Clinton said he had long known Trie because he ran a restaurant in Little Rock near where he lived. He said he had no advance knowledge that Trie was raising the money.
"I saw them start with nothing and build up their family enterprise. They've worked very hard in this country, and they've done well," he said of Trie and his family.

Two weeks after he made the donations, the White House announced Trie had been appointed to a 16-member advisory panel on trade. White House officials denied any connection between the contributions and the appointment.

The disclosure that the money had been returned was the latest post-election embarrassment for Clinton. The Washington Post reported Sunday that Clinton has often let big-time Democratic fundraisers stay overnight in the White House Lincoln Bedroom, among other perks.
For weeks Clinton has been confronted with a steady drip of disclosures about the fundraising tactics of John Huang, a former assistant secretary of commerce for Clinton.

Since the flap began, some $1.5 million Huang raised for the Democratic Party has been returned because it came from questionable sources. Huang's ties to the family of Indonesian billionaire Mochtar Riady have also raised questions. Congressional oversight committees are planning hearings.

The legal defence fund was created in 1994 to help Clinton and his wife, Hillary, pay lawyers for handling various legal problems they have encountered, including the investigation into the Arkansas Whitewater financial entanglement.
